issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not set aside a reasoned order accepting a police closure report merely because another view of the evidence is possible.
material_facts: The police report concluded that there was no evidence to prosecute the public servant, and the competent magistrate examined the case records and accepted the closure report in a reasoned order.

The original complaint attributed the bribe demand to another official; the later allegation against the public servant relied principally on a recorded conversation that forensic examination found inaudible.
The magistrate considered the available evidence and found no sufficient ground to proceed against the public servant.
The High Court set aside the magistrate’s order and directed further steps, relying on a different assessment of the material.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in substituting its view for the magistrate’s without showing a recognized ground for revision; the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and allowed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 173(2), 173(8), 190(1)(b), and 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a magistrate may reject a police closure report and proceed if sufficient ground exists, but the question at cognizance is whether there is sufficient ground to proceed, not whether there is sufficient ground for conviction. Sections 397 to 401 confer revisional power, not appellate power: interference is warranted where the challenged decision is perverse, untenable in law, grossly erroneous, glaringly unreasonable, based on no material, ignores material facts, or reflects arbitrary or capricious discretion. The Court relied on S.K. Sinha, Chief Enforcement Officer v. Videocon International Ltd., Bhushan Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi), Smt. Nagawwa v. Veeranna Shivalingappa Kinjalgi, Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Special Judicial Magistrate, State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, and State of Bihar v. P.P. Sharma; it also noted that unjustified prosecution implicates Article 21.

rule.if: closure_report_accepted_after_record_review and reasoned_magistrate_order and revision_challenges_closure_order and not recognized_revisional_error

predicates.closure_report_accepted_after_record_rev: The magistrate accepted a police report concluding that the evidence did not justify proceeding after examining the case records.
predicates.reasoned_magistrate_order: The magistrate gave reasons for accepting the police report and declining to proceed against the accused.
predicates.revision_challenges_closure_order: A party asked a revisional court to overturn an order accepting a police closure report.
predicates.recognized_revisional_error: The challenged order is perverse, untenable in law, grossly erroneous, glaringly unreasonable, based on no material, ignores material facts, or reflects arbitrary or capricious discretion.

issues.definition: When a magistrate gives a reasoned decision accepting a closure report after reviewing the record, a revisional court may not overturn it merely because it could take another view, absent a recognized revisional error.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not direct the prosecution to seek prosecution sanction when the prosecution has concluded that there is no case and the magistrate has accepted the closure report, unless the court finds otherwise.
material_facts: The investigating agency concluded that there was no evidence to prosecute the public servant and recommended that the case be closed against him.
The magistrate considered the case materials and accepted the closure report against the public servant.
The High Court set aside that order and directed the police leadership to forward the case papers to the competent authority for a decision on sanction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by directing the forwarding of papers for sanction in these circumstances; the Supreme Court set aside its order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 requires sanction for prosecution in the circumstances to which it applies. Where the prosecution considers that no case is made out, a request for sanction serves no purpose unless the court finds otherwise. In Mansukhlal Vithaldas Chauhan v. State of Gujarat, the Court held that a court cannot issue a positive direction compelling an authority to grant prosecution sanction, because that would remove the authority’s discretion to consider whether prosecution is feasible or vexatious.

rule.if: criminal_proceeding_requires_prosecution_sanction and prosecution_concludes_no_case and magistrate_accepts_closure_report and court_directs_sanction_request

predicates.criminal_proceeding_requires_prosecution: The criminal proceeding is one in which prosecution requires prior sanction from a competent authority.
predicates.prosecution_concludes_no_case: The prosecution concludes that the available evidence does not justify prosecuting the accused.
predicates.magistrate_accepts_closure_report: The magistrate accepts the closure report after considering the case materials and does not find otherwise.
predicates.court_directs_sanction_request: A court directs the prosecution or investigating agency to seek a sanction decision despite the accepted closure of the case.

issues.definition: When prosecution requiring sanction has been found unsupported and the magistrate accepts the closure report, a court must not direct the prosecution to seek sanction.

issues.legal_issue: A translation of a recorded conversation cannot be relied on as authentic electronic evidence when the recording is inaudible, the recording device has not been analysed, and the purported verifying witnesses did not hear the conversation.
material_facts: The allegation against the public servant depended on a conversation recorded by a voice recorder.
The forensic laboratory reported that the conversation was inaudible and did not conduct spectrographic analysis of it.
The panch witnesses had not heard the conversation because they were not present in the room.
The recording device itself was not subjected to analysis, while the prosecution relied on a translated version of the conversation.
issues.conclusion: The translated conversation lacked an authenticated source and could not be relied on to establish the allegation.
issues.legal_principle: Electronic evidence requires source and authenticity. Applying Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer, the Court held that a translated version could not be relied on in the absence of an analysed recording and witnesses who had heard the conversation.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_relies_on_recorded_: The prosecution relies on a recorded conversation to support an allegation in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.recording_is_inaudible: The recording cannot be heard clearly enough to establish what was said.
predicates.recording_device_not_analysed: The device or recording has not been examined to authenticate the source or contents of the conversation.
predicates.verifying_witnesses_did_not_hear_convers: The witnesses offered to verify the conversation were not present to hear it themselves.

issues.definition: A translated conversation is not reliable as authentic evidence when the prosecution relies on a recording that is inaudible and unauthenticated and the proposed verifying witnesses did not hear it.
